title: Pizza phone orders: halves, toppings, and sizes
seoTitle: Pizza phone order tips for busy shops | ROAL
description: Handle pizza phone orders with clear questions about halves, toppings, sizes, ready times, and repeat-backs that reduce mistakes.
question: How should I take a pizza phone order so halves, toppings, and sizes are clear and correct?
answer: Take the size first, then crust, sauce, cheese, halves, toppings, and any special notes. Repeat the order back in the same order, confirm the name and phone number, and give a ready time before ending the call. If the order is complex, hand it to staff with a written summary so the kitchen gets it right.
summary: You’ll know how to take cleaner pizza phone orders and reduce mistakes with a simple phone flow.
intro:
A good pizza phone order starts with the size, then the crust, halves, toppings, and any special notes. Say the order back before you hang up, and you will cut down on kitchen mistakes.

That matters most when the phone rings during a dinner rush. ROAL handles that flow for pizza shops by taking orders from your live menu, confirming the details, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What should I ask first on a pizza phone order?
sections.body:
Start with the details that change the price and the build. For pizza, that usually means size first, then crust or style, then the number of pies, then halves and toppings.

A simple phone script helps staff stay calm:
- "What size pizza would you like?"
- "Is that one pizza or more than one?"
- "Any half-and-half toppings?"
- "Any crust, sauce, or cheese changes?"

A clean order flow for a standard pie:
1. Size
2. Quantity
3. Crust or style
4. Sauce and cheese changes
5. Halves and toppings
6. Pickup or delivery
7. Name and phone number
8. Ready time

If you ask toppings before size, the call gets messy fast. A caller may say "pepperoni and sausage" before you know whether they mean a small or large pie. Size first keeps the ticket clear and the price easier to confirm.

sections.h2: How do I handle halves without confusion?
sections.body:
Halves are where pizza orders often go wrong. The best habit is to name the left half and right half the same way every time, and repeat it back slowly.

Use a fixed script like this: "Half pepperoni, half mushroom on a large hand-tossed pizza. Did I get that right?" If your team uses left and right, say it both ways: "Left side pepperoni, right side mushroom."

A helpful kitchen note is to write halves in a consistent format. Example:
| Pizza | Half 1 | Half 2 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Large thin crust | Pepperoni | Mushroom | Light cheese |
| Medium regular | Sausage | Onion | No olives |

If a caller wants three toppings on one half and one topping on the other, slow down and repeat each side. It is better to spend ten extra seconds on the phone than send a pie out wrong. ROAL can take these modifiers from your live menu and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: How do I quote toppings and upsells without sounding pushy?
sections.body:
Keep it short and tied to the order. A useful line is: "Would you like any extra toppings on that pie?" If the caller already named a pizza, ask one follow-up question only when it matters.

Here is a practical upsell ladder for pizza phone orders:
- Ask about extra cheese after the base pizza is chosen
- Ask about premium toppings only if they fit the pie
- Ask about wings, salads, or drinks after the pizza is confirmed

Worked example with numbers you can swap for your own:
- Say a large pizza is $18
- Extra cheese adds $2
- One topping adds $2
- A half-and-half split has no extra charge in your shop, if that is your policy

That means a caller who starts with one large plain pie may end at $22 before tax, if they add cheese and one topping. Use your own prices, but keep the same order of questions. The goal is to make the call feel easy, not salesy.

sections.h2: What is the best way to confirm sizes, toppings, and ready time?
sections.body:
Repeat the whole order in one clean block. This is where many mistakes get caught. Keep the language plain and speak in the same order the kitchen uses.

A strong repeat-back sounds like this: "I have one large hand-tossed pizza, half pepperoni and half mushroom, extra cheese, pickup under Maria, and it will be ready in about 20 minutes."

Use a short confirmation checklist:
- Size is correct
- Crust is correct
- Halves are correct
- Toppings are correct
- Special notes are included
- Name and phone number are correct
- Pickup or delivery is correct
- Ready time is understood

For ready times, quote what your kitchen can actually handle. If your normal pizza turnaround is 20 minutes at lunch and longer during dinner, use the time you can stand behind. If a caller asks for a special request, add a little buffer and tell them clearly. ROAL does this by confirming the order back, collecting the caller name and phone, and quoting a ready time before it ends the call.

sections.h2: How should I price pizza phone orders and compare the cost to other channels?
sections.body:
Phone orders should be easy to compare with delivery apps, monthly phone tools, and human answering help. The cleanest way is to look at the cost per completed order.

ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free. That makes it easier to compare with other options that charge whether orders come in or not.

Use this simple math with your own numbers:
- Say 100 completed phone orders in a month
- 100 x $0.90 = $90
- If your average ticket is $28, that is $2,800 in phone-order sales handled

For comparison, delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order. On a $28 order, that can mean about $4.20 to $8.40 gone from that sale, before other costs. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call, and many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599. Plug in your own numbers and compare the total, not just the headline price. For a quick estimate, [use the AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator).

sections.h2: What should I do when the order gets complicated or the caller needs help?
sections.body:
Not every pizza call should stay on autopilot. Some calls belong with staff, especially allergy-sensitive questions, catering, complaints, or a manager request.

A good handoff line is: "I’m going to pass this to the team with a quick summary." Then the caller is not left guessing.

Use this handoff checklist:
- Allergy or ingredient safety question
- Catering request or large party order
- Complaint about a past order
- Special note that affects cooking or packing
- Caller asks for a manager

For example, if a caller says, "My child is allergic to dairy and we need to be careful," do not guess. Send it to staff with a summary. The same goes for sold-out items. A phone host should not offer items marked sold out, and if the question goes beyond the menu, it should go to the team. This is also where ROAL is useful: it takes the routine pizza order, but tricky calls go to staff with context instead of being lost in voicemail.

sections.h2: How do I set this up on my current phone line?
sections.body:
Start with your website, Google Maps link, or your restaurant name and city. ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages and builds a phone host in about two minutes. You can test-call it right in the browser before you go live.

Going live is straightforward:
1. Claim the host
2. Get the location’s phone line from ROAL
3. Forward your existing number to that line
4. Choose all calls, or only busy and unanswered calls
5. Test it with a real call

On many landlines and some carriers, *72 followed by the forwarding number turns on forwarding and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72, *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. If you want to see the setup flow first, [build a free test host](/try).

takeaways: Ask for size first, then crust, halves, and toppings.
Repeat pizza orders back in the same order the kitchen uses.
Use clear handoff rules for allergies, complaints, and catering.
Compare per-order cost against delivery app commission and monthly phone fees.
Test-call the host and your forwarding setup before relying on it.

faq.q: How do I take a pizza phone order correctly?
faq.a: Ask for the size first, then crust, halves, toppings, and any special notes. Repeat the full order back, confirm the name and phone number, and give a ready time before hanging up.

faq.q: What do I say when a caller wants half and half toppings?
faq.a: Use a simple script: "Half pepperoni, half mushroom on a large pizza." If needed, name the sides as left and right so the kitchen writes it the same way every time.

faq.q: Should I confirm the order before ending the call?
faq.a: Yes. Repeat the size, crust, halves, toppings, name, phone number, and ready time in one short block. That is the easiest way to catch mistakes before the pizza gets made.
